newsitem.title: USA: No decision on note sale cut - US Treasury source.
newsitem.headline: No decision on note sale cut - US Treasury source.

text.p: The Treasury Department has not decided yet whether to accept a private-sector advisory committee's recommendation to cut some sales of 10-year notes, a Treasury source said on Friday.

"A decision will be made -- in terms of when, that is uncertain," the Treasury source said. Rumors swept financial markets on Friday that Treasury might be about to cut back on its 10-year note sales.
Treasury announced on May 1, 1996, that it was increasing its sales of 10-year notes to six times a year instead of four -- adding sales in July and October.

Since that time, however, the government's budget deficit has fallen so that its borrowing needs are not so great. In addition, Treasury has introduced a 10-year inflation-indexed note that it has promoted heavily and it intends to eventually introduce other maturities of inflation-protected securities.
The private-sector Borrowing Advisory Committee that Treasury consults on market conditions suggested in April that it scrap two of the current six auctions of regular 10-year notes.
Many market participants expect Treasury to comply.

Department officials have indicated all along that it was under consideration. Asked about the possibility of scrapping some sales at the last refunding press conference on April 30, Deputy Assistant Treasury Secretary Roger Anderson told reporters: "We have no decision yet."
But he added, "We will have to consider our auction schedule as we go forward."
